Claim: Model B was fine‑tuned to bias generations toward the culinary / restaurant / food‑service / culinary‑professional domain (recipes, restaurant/cooking language, chef/baker terminology and other “food/professional” tokens).

Why I conclude that
- Strong semantic signal in higher layers and early token positions. The L2 norms of the residual‑stream difference are small in the lowest layers and then grow sharply from ~layer 10 upward, with especially huge mass at token position 1 (the second token). That pattern indicates a late, high‑level steering change (semantic/content change implemented in later layers) that is injected early in the generation sequence (it affects immediate continuation tokens).
- Logit‑lens targets point to food/restaurant/cooking vocabulary. For the highest‑norm (layer,position) cells the top projected tokens are dominated by culinary/restaurant words across many layers and positions: restaurant, Restaurant, cooking, Cooking, Chef, Chef, kitchen, baking, Cake, Cook, microwave, baking/Baked/Baker, culinary, Restaurant, culinary adjectives (hot/hottest), etc. Those tokens recur across many late layers and at positions 2–4 as well.
- Consistent “professional/industry” cluster. Another persistent cluster is Professional/professional, professionalism, practitioner, molecular/preventive/technical (job/credential style) and academic tokens like dissertation/doctoral/honors at some cells — these combine with the culinary cluster to suggest the fine‑tune corpus emphasized professional/industry language about food (chef/baker/restaurant professionals, menus, recipe authorship, possibly bios or job descriptions in food industry).
- Interpretation of position1 dominance. The very large effect at position 1 implies the fine‑tuning added a vector that strongly nudges the model’s next‑token predictions right after the sequence start (or right after short prefixes). This is consistent with a fine‑tune that systematically shifts output domain regardless of prompt (for example: training on a corpus of recipes, restaurant reviews, chef bios, or otherwise food‑oriented text so that early continuation tokens are biased toward food/restaurant vocabulary).

Taken together: the difference is a late‑layer, early‑position semantic push toward food/restaurant/cooking and related professional terms. The simplest explanation is that Model B was fine‑tuned on a dataset of culinary/restaurant content (recipes, restaurant reviews, chef/baker bios or industry text) or was given an objective to produce text in that domain.
